description: Portuguese conversation core, part 1 of 2, A2–B1, Brazilian Portuguese

terms.definition: Says what someone or something is: identity, job, origin, or a lasting trait.
terms.example: Sou engenheira, sou de Recife. — I'm an engineer, from Recife.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Eu sou cansado' for 'I'm tired': a feeling right now takes estar, so 'Estou cansado'.

terms.definition: Your everyday 'you' for one person; its verb form is the same as for ele or ela.
terms.example: Você quer um café? — Do you want a coffee?
terms.discussion: Tu is common in the South and Northeast, often with você's verb form. For older strangers, o senhor or a senhora is more polite.

terms.definition: Asks 'what?' about a thing or an action.
terms.example: O que você vai comer? — What are you going to eat?
terms.discussion: At the very end of a sentence it takes an accent: 'Você quer o quê?'

terms.definition: Joins two ideas that pull in opposite directions, like English 'but'.
terms.example: Quero ir, mas estou sem dinheiro. — I want to go, but I'm broke.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Quero ir, mais estou sem dinheiro': mais means 'more'. In Brazil they sound alike, so watch the spelling.

terms.definition: Covers both 'do' and 'make': dinner, homework, sport, a favor.
terms.example: Ontem eu fiz o jantar para todos. — Yesterday I made dinner for everyone.
terms.discussion: It also gives weather and time ago: 'Faz calor' (it's hot), 'faz dois anos' (two years ago).

terms.definition: Asks 'how's it going?', and also answers it: 'all good'.
terms.example: Tudo bem? Tudo, e você? — All good? Yes, and you?
terms.discussion: After an apology it means 'it's okay': 'Desculpa!' 'Tudo bem.'

terms.definition: Tells where someone is, or how someone or something is right now.
terms.example: Onde você está? Estou no ônibus. — Where are you? I'm on the bus.
terms.mental_model: Ser is the label on the box; estar is a photo of the box right now.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Sou no trabalho' for 'I'm at work': being somewhere takes estar, so 'Estou no trabalho'.

terms.definition: Means 'my', and it agrees with the thing you own, not with you.
terms.example: Essa é minha irmã, Ana. — This is my sister, Ana.
terms.anti_example: A man says 'minha casa', not 'meu casa': casa is feminine, and that decides it.

terms.definition: Stands for 'nothing', or 'anything' in a negative sentence.
terms.example: Não tem nada na geladeira. — There's nothing in the fridge.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Eu comi nada': keep não before the verb, so 'Eu não comi nada'.

terms.definition: Gives the reason for something, like 'because'.
terms.example: Cheguei tarde porque perdi o ônibus. — I was late because I missed the bus.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Porque você está triste?' for 'why?': the question is 'Por que…?', two words.

terms.definition: Talks about the future the everyday way: 'going to' do something.
terms.example: Amanhã eu vou visitar minha avó. — Tomorrow I'm going to visit my grandma.
terms.discussion: In speech this replaces the textbook future: 'vou comer' is normal, while 'comerei' sounds like a news report.

terms.definition: Expresses what you want, a thing or an action: 'quero um café', 'quero dormir'.
terms.example: Eu queria um pão de queijo, por favor. — I'd like a cheese bread, please.
terms.discussion: 'Quero' is fine with friends; 'queria' (literally 'I wanted') softens a request in shops.

terms.definition: Counts occasions, like 'time' in 'one time, two times': uma vez, duas vezes.
terms.example: Já fui a Salvador duas vezes. — I've been to Salvador twice.
terms.anti_example: Not 'três tempos' for 'three times': occasions are vezes; tempo is clock time or weather.

terms.definition: Means 'have': things, age, family, plans.
terms.example: Tenho dois irmãos e um cachorro. — I have two brothers and a dog.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Sou 30 anos' for 'I'm 30': age uses ter, so 'Tenho 30 anos'.

terms.definition: Spoken 'we'; its verb takes the ele/ela form.
terms.example: A gente vai à praia no sábado. — We're going to the beach on Saturday.
terms.anti_example: Not 'a gente vamos': the verb stays singular, so 'a gente vai'.

terms.definition: Opens a question about place: 'where?'.
terms.example: Onde fica o banheiro? — Where's the bathroom?
terms.discussion: For 'where to?' Brazilians often say 'aonde' or 'pra onde': 'Pra onde você vai?'

terms.definition: Draws a conclusion, like 'so': one thing happens, and this follows.
terms.example: Está chovendo, então vamos de táxi. — It's raining, so let's take a taxi.
terms.discussion: It also starts a story or fills a pause, just like 'So…' in English.

terms.definition: Know a fact, or know how to do something.
terms.example: Você sabe a senha do wi-fi? — Do you know the wifi password?
terms.anti_example: Not 'Você sabe a Maria?' for knowing a person: that's 'Você conhece a Maria?'

terms.definition: Describes a thing or person as good; boa for feminine nouns.
terms.example: Esse restaurante é muito bom. — This restaurant is really good.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Estou bom' for 'I'm well': how you feel is bem, so 'Estou bem'.

terms.definition: Says 'there is' or 'there are' in everyday speech.
terms.example: Tem uma padaria na esquina. — There's a bakery on the corner.
terms.discussion: In writing and formal speech you see 'há' instead: 'Há uma padaria na esquina.'

terms.definition: Points to a thing near you or just mentioned: 'this' or 'that' before a noun.
terms.example: Essa camiseta é muito bonita. — This T-shirt is really nice.
terms.discussion: In speech Brazilians use esse for both 'this' and 'that'; este shows up mostly in writing.

terms.definition: Means 'nobody' or 'no one'.
terms.example: Liguei, mas ninguém atendeu. — I called, but nobody answered.
terms.anti_example: After the verb, add não: 'Não vi ninguém', not 'Vi ninguém'.

terms.definition: Can: be able or be allowed to do something.
terms.example: Posso pagar com cartão? — Can I pay by card?
terms.discussion: 'Pode' alone is a quick 'go ahead' or 'sure': 'Posso sentar aqui?' 'Pode.'

terms.definition: Adds 'also' or 'too'.
terms.example: Eu também quero ir! — I want to go too!
terms.discussion: For 'me neither' or 'not … either', use 'também não': 'Eu também não sei.'

terms.definition: Says 'thank you'; it literally means 'obliged', so it matches the speaker's gender.
terms.example: Muito obrigada pelo café! — Thanks a lot for the coffee!
terms.anti_example: Not 'obrigado' from a woman because she's thanking a man: she always says 'obrigada'.

terms.definition: Know a person or a place, or meet someone for the first time.
terms.example: Você já conhece o Rio? — Have you been to Rio yet?
terms.discussion: 'Prazer em conhecer' is 'nice to meet you'.

terms.definition: 'I' in Portuguese; often dropped, since the verb ending already shows who.
terms.example: Quem quer mais bolo? Eu! — Who wants more cake? Me!
terms.discussion: After a preposition it becomes mim: 'para mim' (for me). 'With me' is comigo.

terms.definition: Asks 'who?' about a person.
terms.example: Quem vai levar as crianças? — Who's taking the kids?
terms.discussion: 'De quem' asks 'whose?': 'De quem é essa bolsa?'

terms.definition: Describes an action happening right now: 'I'm driving', 'she's working'.
terms.example: Não posso falar, estou dirigindo. — I can't talk, I'm driving.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Estou trabalhando amanhã' for a plan: say 'Vou trabalhar amanhã' or 'Trabalho amanhã'.

terms.definition: Tells where a building, city or shop is located.
terms.example: O hotel fica perto da praia. — The hotel is near the beach.
terms.discussion: It also means 'stay' (fiquei em casa) and 'become' (ficou nervoso); both are very common.

terms.definition: Turns 'you' (você) into 'your'; sua, seus, suas follow the thing owned.
terms.example: Esse é o seu celular? — Is this your phone?
terms.discussion: Seu can also mean 'his' or 'her', so for those Brazilians usually say dele or dela.

terms.definition: Sets a condition, like English 'if'.
terms.example: Se você quer, eu te levo. — If you want, I'll take you.
terms.discussion: Don't mix it up with the se in 'como se diz?' ('how do you say?'): same spelling, different word.

terms.definition: Gives your opinion: 'acho que…' is the normal 'I think…'.
terms.example: Acho que vai chover hoje. — I think it's going to rain today.
terms.anti_example: For opinions, 'Eu penso que…' sounds stiff; Brazilians say 'Eu acho que…'.

terms.definition: Tells how something is done or how someone feels: 'well', 'fine'.
terms.example: Estou bem, obrigado. Dormi bem. — I'm fine, thanks. I slept well.
terms.discussion: Before an adjective it means 'really': 'bem caro' is 'really expensive'.

terms.definition: Puts 'never' before the verb, with no não needed.
terms.example: Nunca comi açaí. — I've never had açaí.

terms.definition: Points to a thing or idea without naming it: 'this', 'that'.
terms.example: Isso é muito caro para mim. — That's too expensive for me.
terms.discussion: 'Isso!' on its own means 'exactly!' or 'that's it!'

terms.definition: Expresses need, for things or for actions.
terms.example: Preciso de ajuda com a mala. — I need help with the suitcase.
terms.anti_example: Before a verb, drop de: 'Preciso sair', not 'Preciso de sair'.

terms.definition: Marks something as 'still' going on, or not done 'yet' in a negative sentence.
terms.example: Ainda não almocei. — I haven't had lunch yet.
terms.anti_example: 'Not yet' is 'ainda não', not 'já não': 'já não' means 'no longer'.

terms.definition: Any object, idea or matter: 'thing'.
terms.example: Tenho muita coisa para fazer hoje. — I have lots to do today.
terms.discussion: It's feminine (uma coisa), and 'muita coisa' in the singular is the usual 'a lot of things'.

terms.definition: Stands for 'he', or 'it' for a masculine noun.
terms.example: O João? Ele está na academia. — João? He's at the gym.
terms.discussion: In speech it's also the object: 'Eu vi ele ontem' (I saw him) is normal.

terms.definition: Wants to know the time of something: 'when?'.
terms.example: Quando você volta de viagem? — When are you back from your trip?
terms.discussion: Without a question it joins clauses: 'Quando eu chego, eu ligo.'

terms.definition: Puts an obligation on someone: 'have to', 'must'.
terms.example: Tenho que acordar cedo amanhã. — I have to wake up early tomorrow.
terms.discussion: 'Ter de' means the same and sounds a bit more formal.

terms.definition: Go, to a place or to an event.
terms.example: Fui ao mercado de manhã. — I went to the market this morning.
terms.discussion: With transport use de: 'ir de ônibus', 'ir de carro', but 'ir a pé' (on foot).

terms.definition: Shows 'his' (de + ele); dela is 'her', deles and delas are 'their'.
terms.example: Esse carro é dele, não é meu. — That car is his, not mine.
terms.discussion: It goes after the noun: 'o carro dele' is 'his car'.

terms.definition: Links a second clause, like 'that' or 'who': 'acho que…', 'o filme que…'.
terms.example: O filme que vi ontem é ótimo. — The film I saw yesterday is great.
terms.anti_example: Not 'O filme eu vi ontem': English can drop 'that', but Portuguese keeps que.

terms.definition: Expresses liking, with de before the thing liked.
terms.example: Você gosta de samba? — Do you like samba?
terms.anti_example: Not 'Eu gosto samba': keep de, so 'Eu gosto de samba'.

terms.definition: Brazil's everyday 'cool' or 'nice', for things, plans and news.
terms.example: Que legal! Parabéns pelo emprego novo! — How cool! Congrats on the new job!
terms.discussion: It works for people too: 'Ele é muito legal' is 'He's really nice'.

terms.definition: Negates a noun: 'no' or 'not any'; nenhuma for feminine nouns.
terms.example: Não tem nenhum ônibus agora. — There's no bus now.

terms.definition: Points to something far from you and the listener: 'that … over there'.
terms.example: Aquele prédio ali é o meu trabalho. — That building over there is my work.

terms.definition: Gives advice ('should') or makes a guess ('must be').
terms.example: Você deve beber mais água. — You should drink more water.
terms.discussion: 'Deve ser' is 'it must be': 'Deve ser a Ana.'

terms.definition: 'Already', or 'ever' in questions.
terms.example: Você já comeu feijoada? — Have you ever had feijoada?
terms.discussion: 'Já volto' means 'back in a minute'.

terms.definition: Agrees or accepts: 'okay', 'fine'. Tá is spoken está.
terms.example: Às oito, tá bom? — At eight, okay?
terms.discussion: Tone matters: a flat 'tá bom…' can mean 'fine, whatever'.

terms.definition: 'She', or 'it' for a feminine thing.
terms.example: A chave? Ela está na bolsa. — The key? It's in the bag.

terms.definition: Gets at manner or description: 'how?' or 'what … like?'.
terms.example: Como é o seu chefe? — What's your boss like?
terms.discussion: 'Como?' on its own asks someone to repeat: 'Sorry, what?'

terms.definition: Places an action a moment ago: 'I've just…'.
terms.example: Acabei de chegar em casa. — I've just got home.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Só cheguei' for 'I just arrived': that sounds like 'I only arrived'. Say 'Acabei de chegar'.

terms.definition: Come, toward the place where the speaker is.
terms.example: Você vem à festa hoje? — Are you coming to the party tonight?
terms.anti_example: Going toward the listener uses ir: 'I'm coming!' is 'Já vou!', not 'Já venho!'

terms.definition: 'Our'; nossa for feminine nouns.
terms.example: Essa é a nossa casa nova. — This is our new house.
terms.discussion: 'Nossa!' alone is the everyday 'Wow!'

terms.definition: Limits something: 'only' or 'just'.
terms.example: Só tenho essa mala. — I only have this suitcase.

terms.definition: Talk, speak a language, or say something to someone.
terms.example: Você fala inglês? Falo um pouco. — Do you speak English? A little.
terms.discussion: 'Fala!' is a casual 'hey!', and 'Falou!' means 'bye' or 'deal'.

terms.definition: 'Very' before an adjective, and 'a lot (of)' with nouns or verbs.
terms.example: Está muito quente hoje. — It's very hot today.
terms.discussion: Before a noun it agrees: 'muita gente', 'muitas coisas'.

terms.definition: Names a thing far away without saying what it is: 'that (over there)'.
terms.example: O que é aquilo no céu? — What's that in the sky?

terms.definition: Say or tell, especially when you report words: 'ele disse que…'.
terms.example: Ela disse que vem mais tarde. — She said she's coming later.
terms.discussion: 'Como se diz …?' asks 'How do you say …?'

terms.definition: Manage to do something, often after some effort.
terms.example: Não consegui dormir ontem. — I couldn't sleep last night.
terms.anti_example: For 'I can't (I tried)', say 'não consigo', not 'não posso', which means 'I'm not allowed'.

terms.definition: Written and careful-speech 'we'; its verbs end in -mos: 'nós vamos'.
terms.example: Nós chegamos às nove. — We arrive at nine.

terms.definition: 'Why?' in a question; the answer then uses porque.
terms.example: Por que você está triste? — Why are you sad?
terms.discussion: At the very end of a sentence it's 'por quê': 'Você não veio por quê?'

terms.definition: 'You' for two or more people; verbs take the eles form.
terms.example: Vocês querem pizza ou sushi? — Do you guys want pizza or sushi?

terms.definition: Makes a sentence negative; it goes right before the verb.
terms.example: Não gosto de acordar cedo. — I don't like getting up early.
terms.discussion: Brazilians often repeat it at the end: 'Não sei não'. That's casual, not a mistake.

terms.definition: Give something to someone.
terms.example: Vou dar um livro para ela. — I'm going to give her a book.
terms.discussion: 'Dá pra…' means 'it's possible to…': 'Dá pra ir a pé?'

terms.definition: Picks from options: 'which?', or 'what?' when there's a choice.
terms.example: Qual é o seu nome? — What's your name?
terms.anti_example: Not 'O que é seu nome?' for 'What's your name?': use 'Qual é…?'

terms.definition: 'They' for men or for mixed groups.
terms.example: Meus pais? Eles moram em Minas. — My parents? They live in Minas.

terms.definition: See or watch something.
terms.example: Vi a Ana no metrô hoje. — I saw Ana on the subway today.

terms.definition: 'How much?'; quantos and quantas ask 'how many?'.
terms.example: Quanto custa a passagem? — How much is the ticket?
terms.discussion: 'Quantos anos você tem?' is how you ask someone's age.

terms.definition: 'They' when everyone in the group is female.
terms.example: As meninas? Elas já foram embora. — The girls? They already left.
terms.discussion: Add one man to the group and it becomes eles.

terms.definition: Take hold of something, or catch transport: a bus, a taxi.
terms.example: Vou pegar um táxi pra casa. — I'm going to get a taxi home.
terms.discussion: Brazilians use it far more than tomar for buses and taxis.

terms.definition: Leave something or someone somewhere and go.
terms.example: Deixei a chave em casa! — I left the key at home!
terms.anti_example: Not 'Deixei de casa às 8' for 'I left home at 8': leaving a place is sair, so 'Saí de casa às 8'.

relationships.description: Both are 'be': ser for what something is, estar for how or where it is now.
Saber for facts and skills, conhecer for people and places.
Bom describes a noun; bem describes how you are or how something is done.
Same sound: porque answers, por que asks.
Conseguir is managing after effort; poder is ability or permission.
'What's your name?' takes qual, not o que.
Vir moves toward the speaker; ir moves away.
Seu is 'your' in speech; dele / dela carry 'his' / 'her'.
Esse is near you; aquele is far from both of you.
Isso is near or just mentioned; aquilo is far away.
'Ainda não' is 'not yet'; 'já não' is 'no longer'.
Dever is advice; ter que is a real obligation.
The present of ir plus a verb gives the everyday future.
Estar plus an -ndo verb shows an action in progress.
The same verb as ter, used with no subject to mean 'there is'.
Both mean 'we'; a gente is the everyday spoken choice.
After the verb, nada needs não before the verb.
